module_title: SMA Succession Rules, Sarla Mudgal & Landmark UCC Judgments
introduction: This intermediate tier explores the complex consequences of marrying under the SMA, specifically regarding property inheritance. It also dives into the landmark Supreme Court judgments that have repeatedly urged the government to implement a UCC.

core_concepts.title: Succession Under the SMA (Sections 21 & 21A)
core_concepts.description:
What happens to your property if you marry under the secular SMA?
- General Rule (Section 21): Succession to the property of any person married under the SMA is governed by the **Indian Succession Act (ISA), 1925** (which is a secular inheritance law), stripping them of their personal religious inheritance laws.
- The 'Two Hindus' Exception (Section 21A): Added by an amendment in 1976. If BOTH parties marrying under the SMA are Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jain, their succession will continue to be governed by the **Hindu Succession Act, 1956**. They do not lose their personal inheritance rights.

core_concepts.title: Severance from Joint Family (Section 19)
core_concepts.description: If any member of an undivided family who professes the Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jaina religion marries under the SMA (with a non-Hindu), their marriage acts as an automatic **legal severance** (separation) from such joint family. They lose their coparcenary status by operation of law.

core_concepts.title: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995)
core_concepts.description:
A landmark case highlighting the need for a UCC to prevent legal fraud.
- The Issue: Hindu men were converting to Islam solely to marry a second wife, circumventing the Hindu Marriage Act's strict monogamy rule.
- The Judgment: The Supreme Court ruled that converting to another religion does not automatically dissolve the first Hindu marriage. A second marriage after conversion, without divorcing the first wife legally, constitutes **Bigamy** (formerly Sec 494 IPC, now **Sec 82 BNS**). The court strongly urged the State to implement Article 44.

core_concepts.title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985)
core_concepts.description:
The most famous UCC-related judgment.
- The Court granted maintenance to a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the CrPC (a secular criminal provision), overriding Muslim personal law which limited maintenance to the Iddat period. Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud observed: 'A common civil code will help the cause of national integration by removing disparate loyalties to laws which have conflicting ideologies.'

important_entities.name: Registration of Existing Marriages (Section 15, SMA)
important_entities.key_fact: Converting a religious marriage into a secular one.
important_entities.significance: A couple already married under religious personal law (e.g., Hindu or Muslim law) can choose to legally register their marriage under Section 15 of the SMA later in life. From that date forward, their marriage is governed by the secular provisions of the SMA.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: An examiner will state: 'A Hindu man and a Christian woman marry under the SMA. Upon the man's death, his property will be divided under the Hindu Succession Act.' **FALSE**. Because it is an inter-faith marriage, Section 21 applies, and the secular Indian Succession Act, 1925 will govern the property. The Hindu Succession Act (Sec 21A) ONLY applies if *both* parties are Hindu/Sikh/Jain/Buddhist.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember that the SMA defaults to secular inheritance (ISA) unless both parties are Hindu, in which case they get to keep the HSA.

exam_strategy_tips: If a UPSC Law Optional question asks you to discuss judicial activism regarding the Uniform Civil Code, you MUST anchor your answer around the triad of **Shah Bano (1985)**, **Sarla Mudgal (1995)**, and **John Vallamattom (2003)**.
